Twenty-five comments

The Kerryman’s Daughter

I learned this from the playing of Eileen Ivers. A simple, straightforward melody that doesn’t need much embellishment beyond the rolls on those long g’s and a’s in the second half. I like to play this before Maids of Feakle, but it works well in front of any reel in G.

If your fingers wear out on the rolls, switch to triplets, but go lightly.

↳ Posted by Will Harmon on October 30th, 2001.

This comes from a banjo player in Yorkshire. One of many great tunes we enjoyed playing together there. Well, he’s much better than I.

This is one of a very few C major tunes we can play on keyless flute. Bothy Band play it in both C and D. The first part is a little bit similar to that of a Shetland reel “Oot Be Est Da Vong,” which is in D.

In O’Neill’s from Patsy Touhey, “Cunningham’s Fancy.” Touhey recorded it announced as “Halligan’s Fancy,” perhaps he’d change the name for each customer buying his homemade cylinder recordings.
Was suprised to find out that this is the same melody as the Banks of Inverness, the first two parts of the Siege of Ennis (from Roche’s collection), the tunes of the songs Paddy Doyle/Doran’s Ass/Mo Ghile Mear. The jig Port tsean-Sean (Old John’s) is the same in 6/8. Kerryman’s Daughter was Coleman’s title.

Re: The Lilting Fisherman

I think things start to go wrong when people spend more time arguing about arguing than they spend time qualifying, backing their assertions. Which may be needed at times since we don’t all see -or hear- things in the same way. Is turquoise green or blue? :: that sort of thing.
I’m not going to launch into a full scale investigation (!), I’m here for the tunes. But, with Erik, I can clearly see the similarity between this here tune and Fred Finn, beyond the same-same introductory notes. And no, I would not say they are virtually identical, that’s an exageration borne out of surprise, I suppose, but their respective melodic contours are similar, regardless of the chord structure involved. Like a seal’s flipper and a bat’s wing, only more similar: Not like a shark’s fin and a seal’s flipper -if you catch my drift. Surely similar enough to warrant a remark.
Fred Finn:
https://thesession.org/tunes/452

There is sometimes a wide discrepancy between what we perceive one tune -or two tunes- to sound like and what they turn out to look like on paper. I think that gap in perception is fascinating and diserves a whole chapter or discussion. To give only one example, I, for a long time truely believed the jig and reel which follow each other on The Bothy Band’s album “Out of the Wind…” were a pair of non-identical jig/reel twins. Turned out the match is far from complete but the initial bars offer enough evidence of identity to trick the mind’s ear to believe so. Like a well practiced conjuror’s trick.

Ref.;
The Leittim fancy (jig)
https://thesession.org/tunes/467
Round the world for sport (reel)
https://thesession.org/tunes/1011

The converse is true; two similar tunes on paper (even tge same) can appear radically different to the ear when presented markedly different.
For example;
when one is played as an instrumental, the other as a song.
when one is played slow the other fast,
or as a reel / hornpipe
high / low
etc.

I hope this helps.
